title: Surdas
hook: a singer by the river stops singing about himself

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tulsidas and the Hanuman Chalisa, which polishes the mirror of the mind and ends with the poet as Hari's servant.

A singer sits near a river and sings about himself. How low he has fallen. How far he is from God. How little he deserves. The songs are lovely, and they are sad. That's how one old account remembers Surdas before his life turned. Tradition says he was blind, and lived beside the Yamuna, in the country of Braj, where Krishna grew up. One day a teacher named Vallabhacharya stops to listen. He hears the sad songs through. Then he says one thing, and it changes what Surdas sings from then on.
screen: `A SINGER BY THE RIVER.` → `SONGS ABOUT HIS OWN FAILINGS.` → `A TEACHER STOPS TO LISTEN.`

segments.voice: The account comes from a book of stories about Vallabha's followers, told in Braj, the language of that country. The teacher says, roughly: why whine like this? Sing about the Lord's play, his lila. And Surdas does. He turns from his own sorrow to a child's life in a cowherd village. The songs carried under his name are called the Sursagar, the ocean of Sur, full of small household things: a cradle, a churn of yogurt, a mother calling her boy in to eat. Here's one. Little Krishna comes to Yashoda with a complaint. Mother, when will my braid grow? You keep telling me to drink my milk and it'll get long and thick like my brother Balarama's. I've drunk and drunk, and it's still short. A tiny boy comparing hair with his big brother, suspecting his mother of a trick. That's the whole song, and it is a song about God. Bhakti has a name for this kind of love: vatsalya, the tenderness of a parent for a child. Instead of looking up at God from far below, the singer stands where Yashoda stands and looks down, at someone small enough to worry about. And the singer's own failings? Nobody told him they didn't matter. He was told to look somewhere else. Tradition says he kept singing in that voice, the voice of mothers and cowherd girls, for the rest of his life.
screen: `WHY WHINE? SING HIS PLAY.` · `THE SURSAGAR: THE OCEAN OF SUR.` · `MOTHER, WHEN WILL MY BRAID GROW?` · then, large: `LOOK DOWN, LIKE A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Notice, without arguing, whatever your mind likes to sing about you: what's wrong, what's late, what isn't enough. Then turn gently, the way the teacher turned Surdas, toward someone small or in your care, a child, a parent, even an animal, and hold them the way Yashoda holds a boy with a short braid: a little worry, a lot of fondness. If you pray, let that tenderness be your prayer.
Surdas. A singer of Braj who, tradition says, was blind, and who turned from his own sorrow to sing of a child named Krishna.
Your line: look down, like a mother. The sad song about yourself can make room for someone small. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Songs from the Sursagar are sung in Krishna temples and homes in north India, and in the Pushti Marg tradition founded by Vallabhacharya they are part of the daily service before Krishna's image.

chat.says: Why would a poet sing about baby Krishna's hair instead of big, serious things?
options: His teacher told him to sing the Lord's play, so he sang with a mother's tenderness.
He was blind, so he could only describe the things children told him about.
Songs about the grown-up Krishna were forbidden to singers in his day.
chat.meaning: Vallabhacharya said, roughly, why whine? Sing his lila. So Surdas sang vatsalya, looking down at Krishna as Yashoda would.

Braj.meaning: the country by the Yamuna where Krishna grew up

Vallabhacharya.meaning: the teacher who told Surdas to sing the Lord's play

Sursagar.meaning: the ocean of Sur: the songs carried under Surdas's name

vatsalya.meaning: a parent's tender love for a child

Yashoda.meaning: Krishna's foster mother in the cowherd village

sources.ref: Chaurasi Vaishnavan ki Varta, the account of Surdas's meeting with Vallabhacharya
Sursagar, the pada in which Krishna asks Yashoda when his braid will grow

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the Varta account: Vallabha's rebuke (often given as 'ghighiyana', whining) and his instruction to sing the lila instead of humility songs.
Surdas's blindness is attributed to tradition, not stated as fact; scholars debate whether he was blind from birth. Confirm the framing.
Confirm the braid pada ('maiya kabahin badhaigi choti') is in the Sursagar as paraphrased, including the milk and Balarama comparison.
'The book of stories ... told in Braj' refers to the Varta, a Braj Bhasha prose work; confirm the description.
howItsDone: confirm Sursagar padas are part of the daily seva (kirtan) in Pushti Marg havelis.
